prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are the standard exclusions. Statement 3 is wrong because receipts from non-relatives can be taxable under other sources, subject to the statutory conditions.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the clubbing of income:
items: Clubbing provisions are intended to prevent the diversion of income to family members who are taxed at lower rates.
Income from an asset transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration is clubbed with the income of the transferor.
The income of a minor child is always taxed in the child's own hands.
Income from an asset transferred for adequate consideration is clubbed with the transferor's income.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 and 2 state the purpose and the main rule. A minor child's clubbable income is taxed with a parent (statement 3 is wrong), and a transfer for adequate consideration is not subject to clubbing (statement 4 is wrong).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding revocable transfers and the transfer of income:
items: Income from an asset transferred under a revocable transfer is clubbed with the income of the transferor.
A transfer is revocable if the transferor can re-assume power over the income or the asset.
Income that is transferred without transferring the asset remains taxable in the transferor's hands.
The clubbing rule for revocable transfers applies only when the transfer is made to the spouse.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1 to 3 are correct. Statement 4 is wrong because the revocable-transfer rule applies whoever the transferee is.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements regarding set-off of losses of the same year:
items: A loss under any head can be set off against income under any other head without any exception.
A speculation loss can be set off only against the profits of a speculation business.
A current-year house property loss can be set off against income of other heads, subject to a statutory limit.
A loss from one house property can be set off against the income from another house property in the same year.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 2, 3 and 4 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong because there are exceptions, for example speculation loss and capital loss cannot be set off against income under other heads.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding interest on securities:
items: Interest on government securities received by an investor is taxed under income from other sources.
Interest on securities is taxable only when actually received, irrespective of the assessee's method of accounting.
If the securities are the stock-in-trade of a dealer, the interest is taxed as business income.
Interest on a bank deposit of a non-business assessee is also charged under income from other sources.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong because the year of taxability depends on the method of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, not only on receipt.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, match List I (receipt) with List II (treatment):
listI: Dividend from a domestic company received by an investor
Gift received from a specified relative
Rent from machinery let on hire that is not business income
listII: Not chargeable to tax as income
No deduction is allowed for any expenditure against it
Taxable in the hands of the shareholder under other sources
Taxable under other sources because it is not chargeable as business income
explanation: Lottery winnings are taxed with no expense deduction, dividend is taxed in the shareholder's hands, a gift from a specified relative is not taxable, and rent of hired machinery falls under other sources when it is not business income.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, match List I (loss) with List II (carry-forward position):
listI: Loss from a source of exempt income
listII: Carried forward for four assessment years
Neither set off nor carried forward
Can be carried forward without a time limit
Carried forward for eight assessment years
explanation: Unabsorbed depreciation has no time limit, a speculation loss is carried forward for four assessment years, a non-speculative business loss for eight, and a loss from an exempt source is ignored altogether.

stem: Match List I (situation) with List II (type of set-off):
listI: Loss from one let-out house set off against the rent of another let-out house
Current-year business loss set off against house property income of the same year
Speculation loss set off against salary income
Last year's unabsorbed business loss set off against this year's business profit
listII: Intra-head set-off
Inter-head set-off
Not permitted
Set-off of a brought-forward loss
explanation: Two houses are two sources under one head (intra-head), business against house property crosses heads (inter-head), speculation loss cannot go against salary, and a loss of an earlier year is a brought-forward set-off.

stem: Match List I (term in clubbing) with List II (meaning):
listI: Income on income from the transferred asset
Transfer of income without transfer of the asset
listII: Income earned on the accumulated income, which is not clubbed
The transferor remains taxable on the income though the asset is not transferred
The transferor retains the right to re-assume power over the income or asset
Two persons transfer assets to each other's spouse or relative, each being treated as the real transferor of his own asset
explanation: A revocable transfer leaves the transferor able to reassume power; in a cross transfer each is treated as the real transferor; income on income is an accretion that is not clubbed; and income assigned without the asset stays with the transferor.

stem: Arrange the following events in the correct order for income arising from a gift between spouses:
items: The wife earns interest on the fixed deposit
The husband gifts money to his wife without consideration
The wife deposits the money in a fixed deposit
The interest is included in the husband's total income under the clubbing provisions
explanation: The gift must precede the deposit, interest accrues only after the deposit, and the clubbing of the interest comes last when the husband's total income is determined.

stem: A business loss of ₹5,00,000 arises in Year 1 and is carried forward. Year 2 business profit is ₹2,00,000 and Year 3 business profit is ₹4,00,000. Arrange the following in the order in which they occur:
items: ₹3,00,000 of the loss remains to be carried forward after the Year 2 set-off
₹5,00,000 of loss arises in Year 1
The balance ₹3,00,000 is set off against the Year 3 profit
No loss remains available for set-off in Year 4
explanation: The loss arises in Year 1 (2), ₹2,00,000 is absorbed in Year 2 leaving ₹3,00,000 (1), the balance is absorbed in Year 3 (3), and nothing is left for Year 4 (4).

stem: Which of the following features most clearly indicates a contract of service (employer–employee relationship) rather than a contract for services?
options: Payment is made to the person through a bank account
The work is carried out at a fixed place
The payer has the right to control and direct how the work is done
The remuneration is fixed for a completed assignment
explanation: The decisive test of a master–servant relationship is the payer's right to control the manner of work (and to dismiss). A fee for a completed assignment points to a contract for services; mode of payment and place of work are not decisive.

stem: Mr K is engaged by a company for specific assignments. He decides how the work is carried out, is free to take other clients and is paid a fee per assignment. His fee is chargeable to income tax under the head:
options: Profits and gains of business or profession
explanation: There is no employer–employee relationship: he works under a contract for services as an independent professional, so his fee is business or professional income, not salary.

stem: Rahul's salary for house rent allowance purposes (basic salary plus eligible dearness allowance) is ₹3,60,000 for the year. He receives HRA of ₹1,80,000 and pays rent of ₹2,00,000. Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, HRA is exempt to the extent of the least of (i) HRA actually received, (ii) rent paid in excess of 10% of salary, and (iii) 50% of salary (the percentage for his city, given as data). The taxable HRA is:

Ms Rekha, covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, retires after 20 completed years of service. Her last drawn monthly salary (basic plus dearness allowance) is ₹26,000 and she receives gratuity of ₹4,00,000. Take 15 days' salary as 15/26 of the monthly salary and the prescribed monetary ceiling as ₹20,00,000. The gratuity taxable under the Income-tax Act, 1961 is:

Mr S, a non-government employee, retires and receives ₹4,50,000 as encashment of accumulated leave. His average monthly salary for the 10 months before retirement is ₹30,000; the cash equivalent of his leave entitlement (at most 30 days per year of service) is ₹3,60,000; the prescribed ceiling is taken as ₹25,00,000. Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the taxable leave encashment is:
explanation: Exemption is the least of (i) ceiling ₹25,00,000, (ii) 10 × ₹30,000 = ₹3,00,000, (iii) leave entitlement ₹3,60,000 and (iv) amount received ₹4,50,000, i.e. ₹3,00,000. Taxable = ₹4,50,000 − ₹3,00,000 = ₹1,50,000.

stem: Mr P, a non-government employee who also receives gratuity, commutes 40% of his pension and receives ₹2,40,000 as the commuted value. Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the taxable portion of the commuted pension is:
explanation: Full value of the pension = ₹2,40,000 ÷ 40% = ₹6,00,000. Where gratuity is also received, one-third of this, ₹2,00,000, is exempt. Taxable = ₹2,40,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹40,000 (₹1,60,000 wrongly applies one-third to the amount received).

stem: Which of the following is a perquisite, as distinct from an allowance or a component of basic salary?
options: Payment by the employer of the employee's personal household electricity bills
Dearness allowance paid monthly in cash
Commission paid to the employee on sales achieved
Monthly basic salary of the employee
explanation: A perquisite is a benefit or facility arising from employment, over and above salary; an employer meeting the employee's personal obligation is the standard example. Dearness allowance is an allowance, and commission and basic salary are direct cash remuneration.

stem: An allowance given by an employer to an employee, in the absence of any specific exemption in the law, is:
options: Not taxable, because it is meant to meet some expense of the employee
Taxable only if it exceeds the employee's basic salary
Treated as a capital receipt of the employee
explanation: Allowances are cash payments added to remuneration and so form part of salary unless the law specifically exempts them (usually only up to the amount spent for the purpose). Their intended use does not by itself make them exempt.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, an employer pays ₹30,000 as income tax on the employee's monetary salary of ₹6,00,000, and also pays ₹12,000 as tax on a non-monetary perquisite valued at ₹50,000. Ignoring deductions, the gross salary of the employee is:
explanation: Tax paid by the employer on monetary salary is itself a taxable benefit (₹30,000), while the tax paid on a non-monetary perquisite is exempt in the employee's hands. Gross salary = ₹6,00,000 + ₹30,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹6,80,000.

stem: Assertion (A): A loan taken by an employee from his employer is not itself taxable as salary.
reason: Reason (R): A loan is repayable by the employee and is therefore not a receipt in the nature of remuneration for services.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Salary is remuneration for service. A loan must be repaid, so it is not income and is not salary (only any concessional interest may be a perquisite). R therefore correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, when an employee receives a lump sum from an unrecognised provident fund, the employer's contributions and the interest on them are taxable under the head Salaries.
reason: Reason (R): The employee's own contributions to the fund are made out of salary that has already been taxed.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both statements are true. R explains why the employee's own contributions are not taxed again, not why the employer's share and its interest are taxed (which is because they are payments from the employer in the nature of profits in lieu of salary).

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, death-cum-retirement gratuity received by a government employee is wholly exempt from tax.
reason: Reason (R): Gratuity is exempt only up to a prescribed monetary ceiling in the case of every employee, government or non-government.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true: government employees' gratuity is fully exempt. R is false because the monetary ceiling and least-of-three limits apply to non-government employees, not to government employees.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, commuted pension received by a government employee is chargeable to tax as salary.
reason: Reason (R): Uncommuted (periodic) pension received by a retired employee from a former employer is chargeable to tax as salary.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: commuted pension of a government employee is wholly exempt (only uncommuted pension is taxable). R is true: periodic pension from a former employer is taxed as salary.

stem: Assertion (A): Salary that has become due to an employee remains taxable even if he later voluntarily waives it.
reason: Reason (R): Once salary has become due the income has accrued, and a later waiver is only an application of income already earned.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Salary is taxed on a due (or receipt) basis, so liability arises when it falls due. A subsequent voluntary surrender does not undo the accrual; it is merely a disposal of income already earned, which is exactly what R states.

stem: Assertion (A): Leave encashment received by an employee while he continues in service is taxable in full as salary.
reason: Reason (R): Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, leave encashment received on retirement by a government employee is wholly exempt.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true. The exemption applies only at retirement or termination; R describes that separate exemption and does not explain why encashment during service is taxed (which is because it is remuneration for services in the nature of salary).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding allowances and perquisites in salary:
items: An allowance is a fixed amount paid periodically by the employer to meet a particular kind of expense of the employee.
A perquisite is a benefit or amenity provided by the employer in addition to salary because of the employment.
A perquisite can be chargeable to tax even though it is provided in kind and not in cash.
Every allowance is wholly exempt from tax because it is meant to meet expenses.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 correctly describe allowances and perquisites. Statement 4 is wrong: allowances are taxable as salary unless a specific provision exempts them (generally only to the extent actually spent for the purpose).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the head 'Salaries':
items: Salary received by an employee from two employers during the year is aggregated and charged under the head Salaries.
Salary includes wages, pension, gratuity, fees, commission and advance of salary.
A fee paid to an independent professional for services rendered is chargeable under the head Salaries.
Wages paid daily to a casual worker by his employer fall outside the head Salaries because they are not paid monthly.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Salary from each employer is aggregated (1), and the statutory meaning of salary includes the items listed in 2. A professional's fee is not salary because there is no employer–employee relationship (3 wrong), and the frequency of payment does not matter (4 wrong).

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements regarding provident fund and salary:
items: Employer's contribution to a recognised provident fund beyond the prescribed percentage of salary is taxable in the employee's hands.
A lump sum received from a recognised provident fund is exempt where the employee has completed the prescribed period of continuous service.
The employee's own contribution to the provident fund is added to his taxable salary.
Interest credited to a recognised provident fund is exempt at whatever rate it is credited.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Excess employer contribution is taxable (1) and the lump sum from a recognised fund is exempt after the prescribed service (2). The employee's own contribution is already part of his salary and is not added again (3 wrong), and interest above the prescribed rate is taxable (4 wrong).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the standard deduction from salary (the amount of the deduction is not in question):
items: It is a flat deduction that does not depend on the expenditure actually incurred by the employee.
It is allowed against income chargeable under the head Salaries, including pension.
It cannot be claimed against income from house property or business.
The employee must produce bills to prove his expenditure in order to claim it.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The standard deduction is a fixed relief from salary and pension income, with no proof of expenditure needed, and it is not available against other heads. Statement 4 is therefore wrong.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding profits in lieu of salary:
items: Compensation received on termination of employment is a profit in lieu of salary.
A sum received from an unrecognised provident fund, to the extent of the employer's contribution and interest on it, is a profit in lieu of salary.
Profits in lieu of salary can be received only from the present employer and never from a former employer.
A payment received from a person before joining his employment can be a profit in lieu of salary.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Termination compensation (1), the employer's share from an unrecognised fund (2) and payments received before joining or after leaving an employment (4) are profits in lieu of salary. Statement 3 is wrong because such payments may come from an employer or a former employer.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements about relief where arrears or advance of salary is received:
items: Because the receipt is taxed in a single year, it may push the employee into a higher rate of tax, and relief is provided for this.
The relief is a deduction in computing income under the head Salaries.
The relief is computed by comparing the tax when the receipt is spread over the years to which it relates with the tax when it is added to the current year's income.
The relief is available only to government employees.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The relief addresses the bunching of income (1) and is worked out by the spread-over comparison (3). It is a relief against the tax, not a deduction from salary income (2 wrong), and it is not confined to government employees (4 wrong).

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (meaning) in the context of salary income:
listII: Salary received before it becomes due
Fixed periodic payment to meet a particular kind of expense
Benefit or amenity, often in kind, given in addition to salary
Salary relating to an earlier period but paid later
explanation: An allowance is a fixed periodic payment for an expense; a perquisite is a benefit over and above salary; advance salary is received before it falls due; arrears relate to an earlier period but are paid later.

stem: Match List I (receipt of a non-government employee) with List II (tax treatment under the Income-tax Act, 1961):
listI: Commuted pension where gratuity is also received
Commuted pension where no gratuity is received
Gratuity of an employee covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
listII: Taxable in full as salary in the year of receipt
One-third of the full value of the commuted pension is exempt
One-half of the full value of the commuted pension is exempt
Exempt up to the least of the prescribed ceiling, 15 days' salary per completed year and the amount received
explanation: Periodic pension is fully taxable; commuted pension is partly exempt (one-third of its full value with gratuity, one-half without); gratuity under the Act is exempt up to the least of three amounts.

stem: Match List I (receipt) with List II (head of income under which it is chargeable):
listI: Pension received by a retired employee from his former employer
Family pension received by the widow of a deceased employee
Remuneration received by a working partner from his firm
Rent received by an employee from a house let out to a tenant
listII: Salaries
Income from other sources
Profits and gains of business or profession
Income from house property
explanation: Pension from a former employer is salary; family pension is taxed as income from other sources; a partner's remuneration is business income of the partner; rent from a let-out house is house property income, even for a salaried person.

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (meaning) in computing house rent allowance exemption under the Income-tax Act, 1961:
listII: Least of the three amounts prescribed by the rule
HRA received less the exempt amount
Basic salary plus eligible dearness allowance and commission on turnover
Amount deducted from rent paid when computing the second limit
explanation: 'Salary' for HRA is basic plus eligible DA and turnover commission; 10% of it is deducted from rent paid in the second limit; the exempt HRA is the least of three amounts; taxable HRA is the HRA received less the exempt portion.

stem: Arrange the following steps in computing the taxable part of commuted pension of a non-government employee in the correct order:
items: Apply one-third (where gratuity is also received) or one-half (where it is not) to the full value of the pension to find the exempt portion
Deduct the exempt portion from the commuted amount received to find the taxable portion
Ascertain the proportion of pension commuted and the lump sum received
Divide the lump sum received by the proportion commuted to find the full value of the pension
explanation: The proportion and lump sum must be known first (3); the full value of the pension is derived from them (4); the exempt fraction is applied to that full value (1); finally the exempt portion is subtracted from the amount received (2).

stem: Arrange the following steps in computing the taxable gratuity of an employee covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 in the correct order:
items: Compute 15 days' salary for each completed year of service
Deduct the exempt amount from the gratuity received to find the taxable gratuity
Take the least of the prescribed ceiling, the formula amount and the gratuity actually received as the exempt amount
Note the completed years of service and the last drawn monthly salary
explanation: The service and salary data are needed first (4); the formula amount is then computed (1); the least of the three figures gives the exempt amount (3); and the exempt amount is deducted from gratuity received (2).

stem: Arrange the following steps in including a perquisite in an employee's salary in the correct order:
items: Include the balance in gross salary
Determine its value under the prescribed valuation rules
Identify the benefit provided by the employer because of the employment
Deduct any amount recovered from the employee for the benefit
explanation: The benefit is identified (3), valued under the rules (2), reduced by any recovery from the employee (4), and the net value is then added to gross salary (1).

stem: Arrange the following events in tax deduction at source on an employee's salary in the correct order:
items: The employer estimates the employee's taxable salary for the year and deducts tax from each payment of salary
The employer deposits the tax deducted with the government
The employer issues a certificate of tax deducted after the end of the year
The employee files his return of income and claims credit for the tax deducted
explanation: Tax is first deducted on estimated salary (1), then deposited (2); after the year the employer certifies the deduction (3), and the employee claims the credit in his return (4).

stem: A house let out for the whole year has municipal value ₹1,20,000, fair rent ₹1,40,000 and standard rent (under the rent control law) ₹1,30,000. The actual rent receivable is ₹1,10,000. Its gross annual value under the Income-tax Act, 1961 is:
explanation: Expected rent = higher of municipal value and fair rent = ₹1,40,000, but it cannot exceed the standard rent, so it is ₹1,30,000. Actual rent (₹1,10,000) is lower and there is no vacancy, so GAV is the higher figure, ₹1,30,000.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, a house is let at ₹20,000 per month and stays vacant for 2 months of the year. Its expected rent for the year (higher of municipal value and fair rent, no rent control) is ₹2,40,000. The rent received for the year is therefore ₹2,00,000. The gross annual value is:
explanation: Actual rent (₹2,00,000) is lower than the expected rent (₹2,40,000) solely because of vacancy, so actual rent received or receivable is taken as the gross annual value.

stem: Mr Ravi occupies his only house for his own residence throughout the year. He paid municipal taxes of ₹8,000, and interest on the housing loan accrued for the year is ₹1,50,000 (assume it is within the maximum allowed for such a house). Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, his income from house property is:
explanation: The annual value of a self-occupied house is nil, so municipal taxes are not deductible and no standard deduction arises. Only interest is allowed, giving a loss of ₹1,50,000.

stem: A let-out house was constructed with a loan. Interest of ₹1,50,000 accrued during the pre-construction period (up to the end of the year before the year of completion). In the year of completion the interest on the loan for that year is ₹60,000. Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the interest deductible in the year of completion is (no ceiling applies):
explanation: Pre-construction interest is allowed in five equal annual instalments starting from the year of completion: ₹1,50,000 ÷ 5 = ₹30,000. Adding the current year's interest of ₹60,000 gives ₹90,000.

stem: Mr A receives ₹1,20,000 as arrears of rent from a tenant in the current year. This rent was not taxed in any earlier year. Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the amount chargeable to tax as income from house property is:
explanation: Arrears of rent are taxable in the year of receipt, after a deduction of 30% of the amount received: ₹1,20,000 − ₹36,000 = ₹84,000, whether or not he still owns the property.

stem: A house is let at ₹20,000 per month for 12 months. ₹40,000 of the rent is unrealised and satisfies all conditions for being excluded. Its expected rent is ₹1,50,000, interest on the borrowed capital is ₹30,000, the owner pays no municipal taxes and the standard deduction is 30% of net annual value. Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the income from house property is:
explanation: Actual rent receivable = ₹2,40,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹2,00,000, which exceeds the expected rent of ₹1,50,000, so GAV = NAV = ₹2,00,000. Standard deduction = ₹60,000; interest = ₹30,000. Income = ₹2,00,000 − ₹60,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹1,10,000.

stem: Where the rent received for a building includes a separable charge for services such as lifts, security and water supply provided by the owner, that charge is:
options: Not income from house property; it is taxed under business or other sources
Part of the annual value of the building and taxed as house property
Exempt, being a reimbursement of expenses
explanation: Annual value covers only the letting of the building. Charges for separable services are not rent for the property and are assessed under business income or income from other sources, as the facts warrant.

stem: A let-out house is owned by two individuals in definite shares of 50% each. Its gross annual value is ₹4,00,000, and municipal taxes of ₹40,000 were paid by the co-owners together during the year. There is no loan, and the standard deduction is 30% of net annual value. The income from the property chargeable to each co-owner is:
explanation: NAV = ₹4,00,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹3,60,000; standard deduction = ₹1,08,000; income = ₹2,52,000. With definite shares, each co-owner is taxed on his share: ₹1,26,000.

stem: Which of the following is NOT separately allowable in computing income from a let-out house property under the Income-tax Act, 1961?
options: Municipal taxes paid by the owner during the year
The standard deduction of 30% of net annual value
Actual expenditure on repairs, insurance and collection of rent incurred by the owner
explanation: Repairs, insurance, collection charges and similar expenses are covered by the 30% standard deduction and are not allowed separately; municipal taxes paid and interest on borrowed capital are separate deductions.

stem: Assertion (A): Where a rent control law applies, the expected rent of a let-out house cannot exceed its standard rent.
reason: Reason (R): Under such a law, the landlord cannot lawfully recover a rent above the standard rent.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Expected rent is the sum a property might reasonably fetch, and a landlord cannot legally charge more than the standard rent, so the law caps expected rent at that level. R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Interest on borrowed capital is deductible for a let-out house even if it has not actually been paid during the year.
reason: Reason (R): Municipal taxes are deductible only when they have been paid by the owner during the year.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true: interest is deducted on an accrual (due) basis and municipal taxes on a payment basis. The rule on municipal taxes is a contrast and does not explain why interest is allowed on accrual.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, arrears of rent received in a later year are taxable in the year of receipt after a deduction of 30%.
reason: Reason (R): Arrears of rent are chargeable under the head Income from other sources.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true: arrears are taxed when received, less 30%. R is false: they are charged under the head Income from house property, not income from other sources.

stem: Assertion (A): Interest on borrowed capital is not deductible in computing the income from a self-occupied house.
reason: Reason (R): The annual value of a self-occupied house is taken as nil.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: interest on a loan for a self-occupied house is allowed as a deduction (subject to the prescribed limit), even though the annual value is nil. R is true.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, a self-occupied house can result in a loss under the head Income from house property.
reason: Reason (R): Interest on borrowed capital is allowed as a deduction although the annual value of such a house is nil.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Starting from a nil annual value and deducting interest leaves a negative figure, i.e. a loss; R therefore directly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The 30% standard deduction on net annual value of a let-out house is allowed even if the owner has spent nothing on repairs.
reason: Reason (R): Interest on borrowed capital is deductible in computing income from a let-out house.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true. The standard deduction is a notional allowance for repairs and collection charges regardless of actual spending; the separate interest deduction has no bearing on why it is allowed.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements regarding the charge of income from house property:
items: The charge is on the annual value of a building together with land appurtenant to it, such as a garage or compound.
A house beyond the number permitted to be treated as self-occupied is deemed to be let out and taxed on its expected rent.
Rent received by a tenant who sub-lets the premises is not income from house property, as he is not the owner.
Only rent actually received is ever taxed under this head; no notional income can be charged.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: the charge is on annual value of the building and appurtenant land, surplus houses are deemed let out, and a sub-letting tenant is not an owner. Statement 4 is wrong because annual value is a notional measure (for example, expected rent of a deemed let-out house).

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements regarding deductions from the annual value of a let-out house:
items: Interest on borrowed capital is allowed on an accrual basis.
Municipal taxes are allowed only if borne by the owner and paid during the year.
The standard deduction is 30% of the net annual value.
Actual repairs are allowed in addition to the standard deduction.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Actual repairs are not allowed separately because the 30% standard deduction already covers repairs and collection charges.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements regarding a house occupied by the owner for his own residence:
items: Its annual value is taken as nil.
The owner can claim the 30% standard deduction on the notional rent of the house.
Interest on borrowed capital can be claimed, subject to the prescribed limit.
Municipal taxes paid by the owner are separately deductible.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Annual value is nil (1) and interest is allowed within the limit (3). With a nil annual value there is no net annual value on which to compute the standard deduction (2 wrong), and municipal taxes are not deductible (4 wrong).

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements regarding unrealised rent:
items: It is excluded from the actual rent receivable only if the prescribed conditions, such as a bona fide tenancy and reasonable steps to recover it, are satisfied.
If recovered in a later year, it is taxed as income from house property in the year of recovery, after a deduction of 30%.
The owner may exclude it from actual rent at his own option without satisfying any condition.
If recovered later, it is exempt because it was already excluded in an earlier year.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Exclusion is allowed only when the conditions are met (1), and the amount recovered later is taxed in the year of recovery after the 30% deduction (2). Exclusion is not optional (3 wrong) and later recovery is not exempt (4 wrong).

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements regarding vacancy and gross annual value:
items: The expected rent itself is reduced in proportion to the period of vacancy.
Actual rent replaces the expected rent only where the shortfall arises from vacancy.
If a house is let at a concessional rent to a relative and is not vacant, the gross annual value is not reduced below the expected rent.
Whenever actual rent is lower than the expected rent, for whatever reason, actual rent is the gross annual value.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The expected rent is computed without regard to vacancy (1 wrong); actual rent is substituted only when vacancy causes the shortfall (2) and a concessional rent without vacancy leaves the expected rent as GAV (3). Statement 4 is wrong for the same reason.

stem: A let-out house has a gross annual value of ₹5,00,000. The owner paid municipal taxes of ₹50,000. Interest on borrowed capital accrued for the year is ₹1,00,000, of which only ₹60,000 has been paid. The standard deduction is 30% of net annual value. Consider the following statements:
items: The net annual value is ₹4,50,000.
The standard deduction is ₹1,35,000.
Only ₹60,000, the interest actually paid, can be deducted.
The income from house property is ₹2,15,000.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: NAV = 5,00,000 − 50,000 = ₹4,50,000; standard deduction = 30% × 4,50,000 = ₹1,35,000; interest is deducted on accrual, i.e. the full ₹1,00,000 (statement 3 wrong). Income = 4,50,000 − 1,35,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹2,15,000.

stem: Match List I (item) with List II (rule for deduction) in computing income from house property:
listII: 30% of the net annual value
Allowed on an accrual basis, whether or not paid
Allowed only if borne by the owner and paid during the year
Allowed in five equal annual instalments from the year of completion
explanation: Municipal taxes are allowed on payment by the owner; the standard deduction is 30% of NAV; interest is allowed on accrual; pre-construction interest is spread over five equal instalments from the year of completion.

stem: Match List I (item) with List II (treatment in computing income from house property):
listI: Unrealised rent satisfying the prescribed conditions
Arrears of rent received in a later year
Separable charges for services such as lifts and security
Shortfall of rent because the house was vacant for part of the year
listII: Taxed in the year of receipt after deducting 30%
Assessed under business or other sources, not as house property
Actual rent replaces the expected rent as gross annual value
Deducted from the actual rent receivable
explanation: Unrealised rent is excluded from actual rent receivable; arrears are taxed on receipt after a 30% deduction; service charges are outside house property; where vacancy causes the shortfall, actual rent is adopted as GAV.

stem: Match List I (situation) with List II (person treated as the owner for house property income):
listI: An individual transfers a house to his spouse without adequate consideration (not under an agreement to live apart)
A member of a co-operative society is allotted a house under its house-building scheme
A person is allowed to take possession of a house in part performance of a contract of sale
An impartible estate with several properties
listII: The holder, in respect of all properties comprised in the estate
The transferor, in respect of the transferred house
The allottee member, in respect of the house allotted
The person in possession, in respect of that house
explanation: These are deemed-ownership rules: the transferor to a spouse remains taxable; the allottee member of a society is owner; a person given possession under a part-performance contract is owner; the holder of an impartible estate is owner of its properties.

stem: Each house below is let for the whole year with no vacancy. Match List I (data) with List II (gross annual value):
listI: Municipal value ₹1,00,000; fair rent ₹1,20,000; standard rent ₹1,10,000; actual rent ₹90,000
Municipal value ₹1,00,000; fair rent ₹90,000; no rent control; actual rent ₹1,30,000
Municipal value ₹1,00,000; fair rent ₹1,20,000; no rent control; actual rent ₹1,10,000
Municipal value ₹80,000; fair rent ₹90,000; standard rent ₹70,000; actual rent ₹75,000
explanation: A: expected rent = higher of 1,00,000 and 1,20,000 = 1,20,000, capped at standard rent 1,10,000; actual 90,000 is lower, so GAV = ₹1,10,000. B: expected 1,00,000 < actual 1,30,000, so ₹1,30,000. C: expected 1,20,000 > actual 1,10,000, so ₹1,20,000. D: expected 90,000 capped at 70,000; actual 75,000 is higher, so ₹75,000.

stem: Arrange the following steps in determining the net annual value of a let-out house in the correct order:
items: Compare the expected rent with the actual rent receivable and adopt the appropriate figure as gross annual value
Take the higher of the municipal value and the fair rent
Deduct municipal taxes paid by the owner to arrive at the net annual value
Restrict the figure to the standard rent, where a rent control law applies, to get the expected rent
explanation: The higher of municipal value and fair rent is found first (2), then limited to standard rent to give expected rent (4), then compared with actual rent to fix GAV (1), and municipal taxes are deducted from GAV to get NAV (3).

stem: Arrange the following events in the treatment of interest on a loan taken to construct a let-out house in the correct order:
items: Interest accrues on the loan during the construction period
Construction is completed
The owner borrows and begins construction
The first of five equal instalments of pre-construction interest is claimed in the year of completion
explanation: The loan is taken (3), interest accrues during construction (1), construction is completed (2), and the pre-construction interest is claimed in five instalments from the year of completion (4).

stem: Arrange the following events in the taxation of rent that a tenant failed to pay in the correct order:
items: The tenant defaults on the rent of a year
The recovered amount is taxed in the year of recovery after a deduction of 30%
The unrealised rent is recovered in a later year
The unrealised rent is excluded from the actual rent receivable of the year of default
explanation: Default occurs first (1); the unrealised rent is excluded when computing that year's actual rent (4); it is recovered later (3); and it is then taxed in the year of recovery less 30% (2).

stem: Arrange the following steps in arriving at and using a loss on a self-occupied house in the correct order:
items: The loss under the head house property is set off against income under other heads of the same year, to the extent permitted
Interest on borrowed capital is deducted, within the prescribed limit
The annual value of the self-occupied house is taken as nil
A loss under the head house property arises
explanation: Annual value is first taken as nil (3), interest is then deducted (2), producing a loss (4), which may then be set off against other heads of income as permitted (1).

stem: The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces the twin concepts of 'previous year' and 'assessment year' with a single period called the:
explanation: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025 income is earned and charged in the same period, called the tax year, so the separate previous year and assessment year of the 1961 Act are no longer used. 'Block period' is an unrelated term from search assessments under the 1961 Act.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, a new business is set up on 1 October 2024. Its first previous year ends on:
explanation: For a business newly set up, the first previous year runs from the date of setting up to the following 31 March, so it is the six-month period 1 October 2024 to 31 March 2025 (assessment year 2025-26).

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, which of the following is NOT one of the heads under which total income is computed?
explanation: The five heads are salaries, income from house property, profits and gains of business or profession, capital gains and income from other sources. Agricultural income is not a head; it is outside the charge (except for rate purposes in partial integration).

stem: Receipts of a capital nature are generally outside the charge of income tax, yet the profit on the sale of a capital asset is taxed. The reason is that:
options: A sale of any asset is always a revenue receipt in nature
Every profit arising from a sale is a casual receipt
The Act treats every receipt in cash as income
The Act specifically brings such gains to tax under the head 'Capital gains'
explanation: A capital receipt is not income unless the statute specifically charges it. The Act does so for gains on transfer of capital assets by creating a separate head, 'Capital gains'.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the affairs of a Hindu undivided family are managed partly from India and partly from Singapore during the previous year. For that year the HUF is:
options: Non-resident unless its karta stays in India for 182 days
Resident only if more than half of its members live in India
explanation: An HUF is non-resident only when the control and management of its affairs is wholly outside India. Control partly in India is enough to make it resident; the karta's stay matters only for deciding whether it is ordinarily resident.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, a company incorporated in India has all its directors and management working from London throughout the year. For that year the company is:
options: Non-resident, because its management is entirely abroad
Resident in India, because an Indian company is resident in every year
Resident only if its place of effective management is in India
explanation: An Indian company is resident in India in every previous year, whatever the location of its management. The place-of-effective-management test applies only to companies not incorporated in India, and the ordinary-residence classification is not applied to companies.

stem: Income is said to 'accrue' to an assessee when:
options: It is actually received by him in cash
It is credited to his bank account
The right to receive it comes into existence, even if it is not yet paid
It is spent or invested by him
explanation: Accrual or arising refers to the stage at which the assessee acquires a right to receive the income (it becomes due). Receipt is a different event: the income actually comes into his hands or is received on his behalf.

stem: A foreign national (not of Indian origin) stays in India for 55 days in the previous year and for 500 days in the four preceding years. Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, his residential status for the year is:
options: Resident, because 500 days exceed the 365-day requirement
Non-resident, because he stayed for fewer than 60 days in the year and fewer than 182 days
explanation: The first basic condition needs 182 days in the year (not met) and the second needs at least 60 days in the year together with 365 days in the four preceding years. With only 55 days in the year the second condition fails even though the earlier stay is long, so he is non-resident.

stem: In the second basic condition of residence of an individual (a stay of at least 60 days in the year together with a longer aggregate stay), the aggregate stay of 365 days is counted over:
options: The two years immediately preceding the previous year
The seven years immediately preceding the previous year
The ten years immediately preceding the previous year
The four years immediately preceding the previous year
explanation: The aggregate of 365 days is tested over the four years immediately preceding the relevant previous year. The seven-year and ten-year periods belong to the additional conditions for ordinary residence.

stem: Assertion (A): A partnership firm is a 'person' under the Income-tax Act.
reason: Reason (R): Under the general law of partnership, a firm has no legal existence separate from its partners.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true because the definition of 'person' expressly includes a firm. R is also true, but it points the other way: tax law treats a firm as a taxable unit by statutory definition, not because of its legal status under partnership law.

stem: Assertion (A): Winnings from a lottery are not chargeable to income tax because such receipts are casual and non-recurring.
reason: Reason (R): The definition of income under the Act includes casual and non-recurring receipts such as winnings from lotteries, races and puzzles.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: being casual and non-recurring does not take a receipt outside income. R is true, since the statutory definition of income expressly covers such winnings, which is why they are taxed.

stem: Assertion (A): The residential status of an assessee is determined afresh for every previous year.
reason: Reason (R): Once an assessee becomes resident in India, he continues to be resident in all later years.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true: residence depends on the facts (stay or control and management) of each year, so a person may be resident in one year and non-resident in the next. R is false for the same reason; residence is not permanent.

stem: Assertion (A): Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, salary paid in London to a non-resident foreign citizen for services rendered in India is taxable in India.
reason: Reason (R): Income from salary is deemed to accrue or arise in India if it is earned for services rendered in India.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Salary for services rendered in India is deemed to accrue in India, and a non-resident is taxed on income that accrues or is deemed to accrue in India, wherever it is paid. R therefore explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The residential status of an individual under the Income-tax Act is determined by his citizenship.
reason: Reason (R): Residential status depends on the individual's physical stay in India during the relevant year and, in some cases, during preceding years.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: citizenship does not decide residence, and an Indian citizen can be non-resident while a foreign national can be resident. R is true, as residence is tested by days of stay in the year and, where relevant, in earlier years.

stem: Assertion (A): A loan received by a trader from a bank is not income in his hands.
reason: Reason (R): A loan carries an obligation to repay, so it adds to the trader's liabilities rather than to his gain.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A loan is a capital receipt. Because it must be repaid, it produces no real gain for the borrower, which is the reason it is not income.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the term 'person' under Indian income-tax law:
items: A company is a person.
Only a natural person can be a person.
An artificial juridical person that does not fall in any other category is also a person.
A body of individuals is a person only if it is registered.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The definition of person is wide: it covers companies and artificial juridical persons (1 and 3 correct). It is not limited to natural persons (2 wrong), and a body of individuals is a person whether or not it is registered or incorporated (4 wrong).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the computation of total income under Indian income-tax law:
items: Income is first computed separately under each head of income.
Agricultural income is a sixth head of income.
Total income is the gross total income reduced by the permissible deductions.
Wholly exempt incomes are left out in arriving at the total income.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Income is computed head-wise, aggregated into gross total income, and then reduced by deductions to reach total income (1 and 3). Exempt incomes are excluded from total income (4). Agricultural income is not a head of income (2 wrong).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the period for which income is taxed:
items: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the income of a previous year is generally assessed in the assessment year that follows it.
Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the income of a tax year is charged to tax for that same tax year.
Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the income of a previous year can never be taxed in that previous year itself.
Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the previous year ends on 31 December.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong because the 1961 Act made exceptions (for example, a person about to leave India or a business being discontinued) where income is assessed in the previous year itself. The previous year ends on 31 March, not 31 December (4 wrong).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding residential status under the Income-tax Act, 1961:
items: The classification 'ordinarily resident' or 'not ordinarily resident' applies only to individuals and HUFs.
The 182 days of stay in India must be continuous for the first basic condition to be satisfied.
A person can be resident for one source of income and non-resident for another in the same previous year.
The additional conditions for ordinary residence are examined only after the person is found to be resident.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Companies and firms are simply resident or non-resident, and ordinary residence is a sub-classification of resident persons (1 and 4 correct). The days of stay need not be continuous (2 wrong), and residential status is fixed once for the person for the year, not source by source (3 wrong).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the meaning of 'income' under Indian income-tax law:
items: Income includes profits and gains of a business or profession.
Income includes dividend.
Income includes the value of a perquisite or profit in lieu of salary.
Income is confined to receipts in the form of money.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The definition of income is inclusive and covers profits and gains, dividend and the value of perquisites (1, 2 and 3). It is not confined to money receipts; a benefit received in kind, such as a perquisite, can be income (4 wrong).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding income deemed to accrue or arise in India:
items: Income from a business connection in India is deemed to accrue or arise in India.
Income through the transfer of a capital asset situated in India is deemed to accrue or arise in India.
Income deemed to accrue in India is taxable for a non-resident only if it is also received in India.
The deeming provisions matter chiefly to non-residents, since a resident and ordinarily resident person is taxed on global income anyway.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: A business connection and an Indian capital asset are standard deemed-accrual cases (1 and 2), and the deeming rules extend the taxable base mainly for non-residents (4). Deemed accrual in India is itself a ground of taxability, so receipt in India is not additionally required (3 wrong).

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (meaning):
listII: The period following the earning year in which the income is assessed
The single period in which income is both earned and charged
The aggregate of income under the heads, before allowing deductions
The period in which the income is earned
explanation: The previous year is the year in which income is earned and the assessment year is the following year in which it is assessed. The 2025 Act merges the two into one tax year. Gross total income is the total of the head-wise incomes before deductions.

stem: Match List I (condition for an individual under the Income-tax Act, 1961) with List II (requirement):
listI: First basic condition: minimum stay in the relevant previous year
Second basic condition: minimum stay in the relevant previous year (supported by 365 days in the four preceding years)
Ordinary residence: minimum number of preceding ten years in which he was resident
Ordinary residence: minimum aggregate stay in the seven preceding years
listII: At least 60 days
At least 2 years
182 days or more
730 days or more
explanation: The first basic condition needs 182 days in the year; the second needs 60 days in the year plus 365 days in the four preceding years. The additional conditions for ordinary residence are residence in at least 2 of the 10 preceding years and stay of 730 days or more in the 7 preceding years.

stem: Match List I (type of person) with List II (description):
listII: A combination of individuals only
An entity treated by law as a person, such as a deity or idol
A family of lineal descendants of a common ancestor, normally represented by its karta
A combination of persons, not necessarily individuals, who join for a common purpose of earning income
explanation: An HUF is a family headed by its karta. An AOP may include non-individual members who combine for a common purpose of earning income, whereas a body of individuals consists of individuals only. A deity or idol is the standard artificial juridical person.

stem: Match List I (term) with List II (meaning):
listI: Income deemed to accrue in India
listII: The right to receive the income comes into existence
Treated by law as received although the assessee has not actually got it
The income comes into the hands of the assessee or of someone on his behalf
Treated by law as arising in India although it may be earned elsewhere
explanation: Accrual is the point at which the right to the income arises, whereas receipt is its coming into the assessee's hands (or his agent's). The deeming provisions treat income as accruing in India, or as received, by legal fiction even though the facts may be otherwise.

stem: Arrange the following steps in determining the residential status of an individual under the Income-tax Act, 1961 in the correct order:
items: Test the additional conditions for ordinary residence
Count the days of stay in India in the relevant previous year and in the preceding years
Classify the individual as resident and ordinarily resident or resident but not ordinarily resident
Apply the basic conditions to decide whether he is resident or non-resident
explanation: The days of stay are counted first (2) and the basic conditions applied to them (4). Only a person found resident goes on to the additional conditions (1), and the final classification as ordinarily or not ordinarily resident follows (3).

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, arrange the following categories of individual assessees in decreasing order of the scope of income taxable in India (widest scope first):
items: Non-resident
Resident and ordinarily resident
Resident but not ordinarily resident
explanation: A resident and ordinarily resident is taxed on global income. A resident but not ordinarily resident is taxed on Indian income plus foreign income only from a business controlled or profession set up in India. A non-resident is taxed only on Indian-source income, so the scope narrows in that order.

stem: Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order for an ordinary assessee under the Income-tax Act, 1961:
items: The Assessing Officer completes the assessment
The previous year ends on 31 March
A return of income is filed for the assessment year
Income is earned during the previous year
explanation: Income is earned during the previous year (4), which then ends (2). The return is filed in the following assessment year (3), and the assessment is completed on the basis of that return (1).

stem: Arrange the following steps in deciding the residential status and tax incidence of a company under the Income-tax Act, 1961 in the correct order:
items: Conclude that the company is resident if that place is in India, and non-resident otherwise
Check whether the company is incorporated in India
Apply the incidence rule: global income for a resident, Indian-source income for a non-resident
If it is not an Indian company, identify where its place of effective management lies during the year
explanation: The first check is incorporation (2); only a company not incorporated in India needs the place-of-effective-management test (4). The residence conclusion follows (1) and the incidence of tax is applied only once the status is known (3).

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, income from a farm building is treated as agricultural income (the other statutory conditions being met) only when the building is:
options: Let out to a trader as a godown for non-agricultural goods
Used by a manufacturer for making non-agricultural products
Situated in a town and occupied by any person who pays rent
On or in the immediate vicinity of the agricultural land and occupied by the cultivator or the receiver of rent-in-kind as a dwelling house, store-house or outbuilding
explanation: A farm building counts as agricultural only when it is on or near the land and is occupied by the cultivator (or the receiver of rent-in-kind) as a dwelling, store-house or other outbuilding required for the land. Letting it out for trade or industry breaks the nexus with agriculture.

stem: Under Indian income-tax law, an exempt income differs from a deduction in that:
options: An exempt income is left out in arriving at gross total income, whereas a deduction is allowed out of gross total income to arrive at total income
An exempt income is allowed out of gross total income, whereas a deduction is left out before gross total income is arrived at
An exempt income is taxed at a concessional rate, whereas a deduction is taxed at the normal rate
An exempt income is available only to individuals, whereas a deduction is available to every assessee
explanation: Exempt incomes never enter the computation of total income, so they are absent from gross total income. Deductions are allowed from gross total income, after the heads have been aggregated, to reach total income.

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, which of the following receipts of a cultivator is agricultural income?
options: Profit from running a flour mill that grinds wheat for customers
Sale proceeds of paddy raised on his own land, after threshing and winnowing it to make it fit for the market
Profit from buying and selling grain in a wholesale market
Income from rearing and selling poultry
explanation: Income from produce raised by the cultivator is agricultural, including the sale of produce after the processes ordinarily employed by a cultivator to make it marketable, such as threshing and winnowing. A flour mill, trading in grain and poultry farming do not have the required direct nexus with land.

stem: Assume that where a person grows tea and manufactures it for sale, 40% of the composite income is treated as business income (data given for this question). A grower earns a composite income of ₹10,00,000 from such tea, after allowing all expenses, and also earns ₹2,00,000 from a transport business. His income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession' is:
explanation: Business part of tea income = 40% of ₹10,00,000 = ₹4,00,000; the other ₹6,00,000 is exempt agricultural income. Business income = ₹4,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹6,00,000.

stem: Assume that where a cultivator grows rubber and manufactures latex-based products from it, 35% of the composite income is treated as business income (data given for this question). He sells such products for ₹20,00,000. The cost of growing the rubber is ₹6,00,000 and the cost of manufacture is ₹4,00,000, both fully allowable. His exempt agricultural income is:

For an individual, assume the basic exemption limit is ₹3,00,000 and the slabs are: up to ₹3,00,000 nil; ₹3,00,001 to ₹6,00,000 at 5%; ₹6,00,001 to ₹9,00,000 at 10%; above ₹9,00,000 at 20%. Ignore rebate, surcharge and cess, and assume partial integration applies. If his non-agricultural income is ₹7,00,000 and agricultural income is ₹2,00,000, the income tax payable is:

Assume partial integration applies to an individual only if net agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000 and non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit of ₹3,00,000. Slabs: up to ₹3,00,000 nil; ₹3,00,001 to ₹6,00,000 at 5%; ₹6,00,001 to ₹9,00,000 at 10%. Ignore rebate, surcharge and cess. An individual has non-agricultural income of ₹6,00,000 and agricultural income of ₹4,000. His income tax is:
explanation: Agricultural income of ₹4,000 does not exceed ₹5,000, so partial integration does not apply and tax is on ₹6,00,000 alone = 5% of 3,00,000 = ₹15,000. (Had it applied, tax would be 15,400 − 200 = ₹15,200.)

stem: A farmer's receipts for the year are: sale of crops grown on his own land in India ₹5,00,000; rent from letting a shed in a town as a shop ₹60,000; interest on a bank deposit ₹20,000; rent from agricultural land in India let to a neighbour for cultivation ₹1,00,000. His agricultural income is:
explanation: Sale of produce raised on the land (₹5,00,000) and rent from agricultural land used for cultivation (₹1,00,000) are agricultural income = ₹6,00,000. Rent from a shop and bank interest have no direct nexus with agricultural land.

stem: In a year an individual's incomes are: business income ₹4,00,000; interest on a bank deposit ₹40,000; share of profit from a firm assessed as a firm ₹1,50,000; agricultural income from land in India ₹2,00,000; and a scholarship of ₹60,000 granted to meet the cost of his education. His gross total income, ignoring any effect on the rate of tax, is:
explanation: The firm's share of profit, agricultural income and the education scholarship are exempt and excluded. Gross total income = business income 4,00,000 + bank interest 40,000 = ₹4,40,000.

stem: Assertion (A): A loss incurred in agricultural operations cannot be set off against non-agricultural income.
reason: Reason (R): Agricultural income is exempt, so the agricultural loss does not enter the computation of total income under the heads of income.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: Both are true. Because agricultural income, and therefore its loss, lies outside the total income, the loss has no place in the set-off that operates among taxable heads. R is precisely why A holds.

stem: Assertion (A): Income of a person who grows tea and manufactures it for sale is treated as partly agricultural and partly business income.
reason: Reason (R): Converting the tea leaf into saleable tea goes beyond the processes a cultivator ordinarily employs to make produce fit for the market.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The manufacturing stage is a business activity, not an ordinary cultivator's process, so the composite income is split by a prescribed percentage between business income and agricultural income. R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): A sum received by a member of a Hindu undivided family out of the income of the family is exempt in his hands.
reason: Reason (R): The karta manages the property and affairs of the Hindu undivided family.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true, because the family income has already been taxed in the hands of the HUF, which avoids double taxation. R is also true but is only about management by the karta and does not explain the exemption.

stem: Assertion (A): Agricultural income is exempt from tax under the Income-tax Act.
reason: Reason (R): The Constitution empowers only the Union Parliament, and not the States, to tax agricultural income.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is true. R is false: taxation of agricultural income is a State subject under the Constitution, which is why the Union's Income-tax Act exempts it (subject to its use for fixing the rate in partial integration).

stem: Assertion (A): Income from the sale of produce by a person who receives the land's rent in kind is agricultural income.
reason: Reason (R): Only a person who personally cultivates the land can earn agricultural income.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: The definition covers income from the sale of produce raised by a cultivator or received as rent in kind, so A is true. R is false because rent or revenue from land is agricultural income even for a landlord who does not cultivate.

stem: Assertion (A): Income from agricultural land situated in an urban area is not exempt agricultural income.
reason: Reason (R): Rural agricultural land in India is not a capital asset for the purpose of capital gains.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
explanation: A is false: rent or revenue from agricultural land in India used for agricultural purposes is agricultural income whether the land is rural or urban. R is true, but the rural/urban distinction matters only for capital gains.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding a Hindu undivided family under Indian income-tax law:
items: An HUF is assessed to tax as a separate person in its own name.
A sum received by a member out of the income of the family is exempt in his hands.
The income of an HUF is assessed in the personal hands of its karta.
An HUF can be created by an agreement between two unrelated persons.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: An HUF is itself a taxable person and a member's receipt from family income is exempt, since the HUF has already been taxed (1 and 2). The karta only represents the HUF; he is not assessed personally on its income (3 wrong). An HUF arises by status under Hindu law, not by agreement (4 wrong).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding agricultural income under the Income-tax Act, 1961:
items: Income from vegetables grown on land by a cultivator after tilling and sowing is agricultural income.
Profit earned by a trader from buying crops from farmers and reselling them is agricultural income.
Income from a fruit orchard planted and maintained by its owner on his land in India is agricultural income.
Interest earned by a farmer on money lent to other farmers is agricultural income.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Growing vegetables and maintaining an orchard are agricultural operations on land (1 and 3). A trader's resale profit is business income (2 wrong), and interest on loans has no direct nexus with the land (4 wrong).

stem: Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, consider the following statements regarding exempt incomes:
items: Expenditure incurred to earn income that is wholly exempt is not deductible in computing taxable income.
Exempt incomes are excluded in arriving at the total income.
Agricultural income is ignored altogether in computing the tax of an individual who also has substantial non-agricultural income.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Cost of earning exempt income cannot be set against taxable income (1), and exempt incomes do not form part of total income (2). Statement 3 is wrong because, under partial integration, agricultural income is taken into account in fixing the rate of tax on the non-agricultural income of an individual.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding income that is partly agricultural and partly business (such as tea, coffee and rubber grown and processed by the same person):
items: The composite income is first computed as if the whole of it were business income, after allowing the expenses.
The portion treated as business income is fixed by percentages prescribed in the Income-tax Rules.
The same apportionment applies to every crop a grower processes before sale.
A grower who sells only raw tea leaves, without any manufacture, has wholly agricultural income.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The composite income is computed first and then split by prescribed percentages (1 and 2). The rules cover only specified crops such as tea, coffee and rubber, not every crop (3 wrong). Raw tea leaves sold without manufacture involve no business process, so the income is wholly agricultural (4).

stem: Assume partial integration applies to an individual only if net agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000 and non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit of ₹3,00,000. Consider the following statements:
items: An individual with agricultural income of ₹40,000 and non-agricultural income of ₹2,50,000 is outside partial integration.
An individual with agricultural income of ₹3,000 and non-agricultural income of ₹8,00,000 is outside partial integration.
An individual with agricultural income of ₹40,000 and non-agricultural income of ₹5,00,000 is within partial integration.
Where partial integration applies, the agricultural income itself is taxed at the slab rates.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: Statement 1 fails the non-agricultural income condition and statement 2 fails the agricultural income condition, so both are outside partial integration; statement 3 satisfies both conditions. Statement 4 is wrong: agricultural income is only added to fix the rate and remains exempt.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding agricultural income under the Income-tax Act, 1961:
items: The exemption for agricultural income from land in India does not depend on the residential status of the assessee.
A company that earns agricultural income has it added to its non-agricultural income to determine the rate of tax.
Partial integration of agricultural income applies, among others, to individuals and HUFs.
Agricultural income earned by a partnership firm is exempt in the hands of the firm.
prompt: Which of the above statements are correct?
explanation: The exemption turns on the land being in India and used for agriculture, not on the residence of the assessee (1), and a firm's agricultural income is exempt (4). Partial integration covers individuals, HUFs and similar persons (3), but not companies, which pay tax at flat rates (2 wrong).

stem: Match List I (receipt) with List II (treatment under the Income-tax Act, 1961):
listI: Share of profit received by a partner from a firm assessed as a firm
Sum received by an HUF member out of the family income
Remuneration received by a working partner from the firm
Scholarship granted to meet the cost of education
listII: Taxable as income from business or profession
Exempt, since the firm has already been taxed on the profit
Exempt, since the HUF has already been assessed on the family income
Exempt, being intended to support education
explanation: A partner's share of profit is exempt because the firm is taxed on it; a member's receipt from family income is exempt because the HUF is taxed on it. A working partner's remuneration is taxable as business income, and a scholarship for the cost of education is exempt.

stem: Assume the business portion of the composite income is: tea grown and manufactured 40%; rubber grown and manufactured 35%; coffee grown and cured 25%; coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground 40%. Match each composite income (computed after all expenses) in List I with the business income in List II:
listI: Coffee grown and cured: composite income ₹12,00,000
Coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground: composite income ₹5,00,000

stem: Match List I (activity or receipt) with List II (classification under the Income-tax Act, 1961):
listI: Growing and selling paddy raised on his own land by a farmer
Running a dairy farm and selling milk
Tea grown and manufactured for sale by the grower
Interest earned by a farmer on a bank deposit
listII: Partly agricultural and partly business income
Income from other sources
Wholly agricultural income
Business income and not agricultural income
explanation: Paddy raised on his own land is wholly agricultural. Dairy farming is not agriculture and is business income. Tea grown and manufactured is split between agricultural and business income. Bank interest has no nexus with land, so it falls under income from other sources.

stem: Assume the basic exemption limit is ₹3,00,000 and the slabs are: ₹3,00,001 to ₹6,00,000 at 5%; ₹6,00,001 to ₹9,00,000 at 10%; above ₹9,00,000 at 20%. Partial integration applies only where agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000 and non-agricultural income exceeds ₹3,00,000. Ignoring rebate, surcharge and cess, match each case in List I with the income tax in List II:
listII: Nil
